source.title: ORLM: A Customizable Framework in Training Large Models for Automated Optimization Modeling
source.authors: Chenyu Huang; Zhengyang Tang; Shixi Hu; Ruoqing Jiang; Xin Zheng; Dongdong Ge; Benyou Wang; Zizhuo Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper and online supplement are present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies training-data volume and model size and measures downstream task accuracy, a different outcome from the original held-out pretraining loss. Its own scaling results bear on the task-performance and fit-dependence versions.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own scaling experiments in Section 5.3 only. Scaling claims cited from Kaplan et al. are not results from this study. The study measures execution accuracy on optimization-modeling benchmarks, not held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.test_reason: Section 5.3 runs its own scaling sweeps in a new setting: task-specific instruction tuning for optimization modeling. It varies fine-tuning data volume for LLaMA-3-8B over 2k–30k examples and base-model size for Qwen2.5 over 0.5B–14B, then reports downstream execution accuracy. These results bear on V6 only. No pretraining loss is measured, so V1–V5 are not tested. The micro/macro contrast concerns how downstream accuracy is aggregated, not fitted loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits, so it is not V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that more fine-tuning data and larger base models improve ORLM accuracy. They call the model-size trend a power law 'consistent with' Kaplan et al., and the micro-average data trend approximately power-law. They note macro-average fluctuation from easy-set plateaus, and in Section 6.2 they note that data gains become increasingly marginal at a fixed model size.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates execution accuracy after instruction tuning on synthetic optimization-modeling data across fine-tuning data volumes and Qwen2.5 model sizes; it does not reproduce pretraining-loss scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data scaling differs between micro and macro averages; the macro average fluctuates and can bottleneck on simpler test sets. The model-size sweep uses Qwen2.5 models and the same training dataset and hyperparameters.
record.peer_reviewed: Operations Research (2025), published online ahead of print
record.problems: The scaling outcome is benchmark execution accuracy after task-specific fine-tuning rather than pretraining loss. The scaling section reports trends without uncertainty estimates; the supplied numerical tables are flattened, preventing reliable assignment of individual values to sweep conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for individual training-data volumes or model sizes: the paper’s text describes aggregate sweep trends, while the supplied numerical tables are flattened and do not reliably support assigning each value to a condition.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No compute-budget allocation between parameters and tokens.
No depth/width or other shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Fine-tuning is studied, but only through accuracy, not a loss power law.
Not tested: prediction from pretraining loss; any fitted functional form or extrapolation; other downstream tasks; model sizes beyond 14B; fine-tuning data beyond about 32k examples.
No variation of parameter counting, schedule or fitting method; no exponents reported.

missing.what: Per-benchmark values for the data-volume sweep. NL4OPT plateaus around 80–82% after 4k examples, and the IndustryOR-like column stays flat at 23–30% with no data trend. Column assignment is uncertain in the flattened table.
Per-benchmark values for the size sweep. The MAMO-ComplexLP-like column rises 16.1%→48.3% and IndustryOR 13%→26% from 0.5B to 14B.
Endpoint points outside the sweep: seed-only data (686 examples) gives 67.0% micro and 51.8% macro; full data (32,481) gives 71.4% micro, below the 30k value of 72.3%.

record.verdict_notes: The 'power law' characterisations are verbal only: no fit, exponent, or uncertainty is reported, and the outcome is bounded accuracy rather than loss. The size sweep uses separately pretrained Qwen2.5 bases, so pretraining data and compute differ across sizes. Table values were read from flattened text; the micro and macro columns match the averages reported in Table 2, but the per-benchmark column assignment is less certain.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit loss curves on small runs or test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not compare parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or fit compute-optimal scaling laws.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
It studies optimization-modeling instruction tuning, not other modalities, repeated-data pretraining, or fine-tuning/transfer scaling in the sense of the version.
Tests optimization-modeling benchmark execution accuracy versus fine-tuning data volume and model size only; it does not test predictability from pretraining loss or other downstream tasks.

The study reports metric-specific differences in the data-size sweep, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, training schedule, or fitting method, report fitted exponents, compare published laws, or test compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: ORLM-LLaMA-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Vary training-data volume while keeping the base model and other hyperparameters fixed; report aggregate benchmark accuracy trend.

conditions.value: micro average across four test sets

rows.value: The overall performance continues to exhibit a monotonic increase with training data and approximately follows a power-law trend.
rows.note: The paper describes the aggregate trend in text. Table 13 is flattened in the supplied text, so individual data-size values are not assigned here.
rows.check: Drop V7: metric aggregation of downstream accuracy is not a loss-law fitting choice. Table 13 is readable. Micro avg (my reading of the flattened columns) is 60.9% at 2k, then 68.9%, 69.3%, 70.4%, 70.9%, 71.6%, 71.7%, and 72.3% at 30k: monotonic. Most of the gain comes from 2k→4k (+8.0 pts); 4k→30k adds only +3.4 pts. No power-law fit or exponent is reported; 'approximately power-law' is the authors' verbal description. Table 2's full-data run (32,481 examples) gives 71.4%, slightly below the 30k value.

rows.subject: ORLM-LLaMA-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Vary training-data volume while keeping the base model and other hyperparameters fixed; report aggregate benchmark accuracy trend.

conditions.value: macro average across four test sets

rows.value: Performance gains fluctuate; the paper attributes this in part to performance bottlenecks and fluctuations on the simpler test sets.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this metric with the micro average, which it describes as continuing to increase approximately as a power law. Table 13 is flattened in the supplied text, so individual data-size values are not assigned here.
rows.check: Drop V7. Values from Table 13: macro avg is 50.1% at 2k, 55.0%, 56.5%, 58.6% at 8k, 57.6% at 10k, 57.9%, 58.6%, and 59.8% at 30k. The overall rise is about 9.7 pts, with one dip (8k→10k). Partial is right: the trend is upward but non-monotonic.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5
rows.size_stated: 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B are tested in the sweep
rows.operation_detail: Compare model sizes using the same training dataset and identical training hyperparameters; report aggregate benchmark accuracy trend.

conditions.value: micro average across four test sets

rows.value: Accuracy increases with model size; the paper characterizes the model-size scaling trend as following a power law.
rows.note: The text describes the overall size-scaling result. The supplied Table 14 layout is flattened, so individual size-specific values are not assigned here.
rows.check: Subject should be ORLM-Qwen2.5 (Qwen2.5 bases fine-tuned on all OR-Instruct data). Table 14 micro avg: 56.6% (0.5B), 66.9% (1.5B), 71.1% (3B), 73.7% (7B), 74.5% (14B). The rise is monotonic with diminishing gains (+0.8 pts from 7B to 14B). No fit is reported.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5
rows.size_stated: 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B are tested in the sweep
rows.operation_detail: Compare model sizes using the same training dataset and identical training hyperparameters; report aggregate benchmark accuracy trend.

conditions.value: macro average across four test sets

rows.value: Accuracy increases with model size; the paper characterizes the model-size scaling trend as following a power law.
rows.note: The text describes the overall size-scaling result. The supplied Table 14 layout is flattened, so individual size-specific values are not assigned here.
rows.check: Subject should be ORLM-Qwen2.5. Table 14 macro avg: 41.5%, 51.6%, 57.0%, 60.1%, 62.0% from 0.5B to 14B. Monotonic; no fit reported.

relationships.condition: OR benchmarks after fine-tuning: data-volume sweep on the micro average; Qwen2.5 size sweep on micro and macro averages
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically with fine-tuning data (60.9→72.3%, R1) and with model size (56.6→74.5% micro, 41.5→62.0% macro; R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased with data from 60.9% to 72.3%, and with model size from 56.6% to 74.5% on the micro average and 41.5% to 62.0% on the macro average.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-3-8B data-volume sweep on the macro average; per-benchmark results
relationships.reason: Macro gains are non-monotonic (58.6% at 8k, then 57.6% at 10k; R2). The authors attribute this to plateaus on the easy test sets. Gains past 4k are small, and no fitted law is given, so 'predictable' is asserted rather than shown.
relationships.display_finding: Macro accuracy fell from 58.6% at 8k examples to 57.6% at 10k, with small gains beyond 4k attributed to easy-test-set plateaus and no fitted predictive law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Aggregate downstream execution accuracy rises with training-data volume on the micro average and with model size; the paper describes the latter trend as power-law-like (R1, R3, R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Macro-average gains fluctuate rather than following the reported monotonic micro-average trend (R2).

reader_labels.reason: The reported scaling behavior differs by aggregate metric: the micro average is described as monotonic and approximately power-law, while the macro average fluctuates and encounters bottlenecks (R1, R2).
